entries.name: find
entries.summary: search for files in a folder tree
entries.explain: Walks a folder tree and prints the files that satisfy an expression of tests. Tests can look at the name, type, size and age of a file. Actions such as exec run a command on every match.
intents: run a command on many files

sections.heading: NAME
sections.body: find - search for files in a folder tree

sections.heading: SYNOPSIS
sections.body: find [folder ...] [expression]

sections.heading: DESCRIPTION
body: Walks each folder named on the command line from the top down and evaluates an expression
for every file it meets. The expression is a chain of tests, actions and operators.
Tests look at one property of a file and answer yes or no. Actions do something with a file.
When the expression has no action, the path of every matching file is printed.
-name
True when the base name of the file satisfies the given value (shell pattern).
A leading plus sign means greater than and a minus sign means less than for name.
Combine -name with the operators -and, -or and -not to build larger expressions.
Tests are evaluated from left to right and stop at the first one that fails.
Use -name early in the expression when it rules out many files cheaply.
-iname
True when the base name, ignoring case of the file satisfies the given value (shell pattern).
A leading plus sign means greater than and a minus sign means less than for iname.
Combine -iname with the operators -and, -or and -not to build larger expressions.
Tests are evaluated from left to right and stop at the first one that fails.
Use -iname early in the expression when it rules out many files cheaply.
-path
True when the whole path of the file satisfies the given value (shell pattern).
A leading plus sign means greater than and a minus sign means less than for path.
Combine -path with the operators -and, -or and -not to build larger expressions.
Tests are evaluated from left to right and stop at the first one that fails.
Use -path early in the expression when it rules out many files cheaply.
-type
True when the kind of file of the file satisfies the given value (single letter).
A leading plus sign means greater than and a minus sign means less than for type.
Combine -type with the operators -and, -or and -not to build larger expressions.
Tests are evaluated from left to right and stop at the first one that fails.
Use -type early in the expression when it rules out many files cheaply.
-size
True when the size of the file satisfies the given value (number with a unit).
A leading plus sign means greater than and a minus sign means less than for size.
Combine -size with the operators -and, -or and -not to build larger expressions.
Tests are evaluated from left to right and stop at the first one that fails.
Use -size early in the expression when it rules out many files cheaply.
-mtime
True when the modification age of the file satisfies the given value (number of days).
A leading plus sign means greater than and a minus sign means less than for mtime.
Combine -mtime with the operators -and, -or and -not to build larger expressions.
Tests are evaluated from left to right and stop at the first one that fails.
Use -mtime early in the expression when it rules out many files cheaply.
-atime
True when the access age of the file satisfies the given value (number of days).
A leading plus sign means greater than and a minus sign means less than for atime.
Combine -atime with the operators -and, -or and -not to build larger expressions.
Tests are evaluated from left to right and stop at the first one that fails.
Use -atime early in the expression when it rules out many files cheaply.
-ctime
True when the status change age of the file satisfies the given value (number of days).
A leading plus sign means greater than and a minus sign means less than for ctime.
Combine -ctime with the operators -and, -or and -not to build larger expressions.
Tests are evaluated from left to right and stop at the first one that fails.
Use -ctime early in the expression when it rules out many files cheaply.
-perm
True when the permission bits of the file satisfies the given value (octal mode).
A leading plus sign means greater than and a minus sign means less than for perm.
Combine -perm with the operators -and, -or and -not to build larger expressions.
Tests are evaluated from left to right and stop at the first one that fails.
Use -perm early in the expression when it rules out many files cheaply.
-user
True when the owner of the file satisfies the given value (user name or id).
A leading plus sign means greater than and a minus sign means less than for user.
Combine -user with the operators -and, -or and -not to build larger expressions.
Tests are evaluated from left to right and stop at the first one that fails.
Use -user early in the expression when it rules out many files cheaply.
-group
True when the group of the file satisfies the given value (group name or id).
A leading plus sign means greater than and a minus sign means less than for group.
Combine -group with the operators -and, -or and -not to build larger expressions.
Tests are evaluated from left to right and stop at the first one that fails.
Use -group early in the expression when it rules out many files cheaply.
-links
True when the link count of the file satisfies the given value (number).
A leading plus sign means greater than and a minus sign means less than for links.
Combine -links with the operators -and, -or and -not to build larger expressions.
Tests are evaluated from left to right and stop at the first one that fails.
Use -links early in the expression when it rules out many files cheaply.
-empty
True when the emptiness of the file satisfies the given value (no value).
A leading plus sign means greater than and a minus sign means less than for empty.
Combine -empty with the operators -and, -or and -not to build larger expressions.
Tests are evaluated from left to right and stop at the first one that fails.
Use -empty early in the expression when it rules out many files cheaply.
-newer
True when the modification time against a reference of the file satisfies the given value (path of the reference file).
A leading plus sign means greater than and a minus sign means less than for newer.
Combine -newer with the operators -and, -or and -not to build larger expressions.
Tests are evaluated from left to right and stop at the first one that fails.
Use -newer early in the expression when it rules out many files cheaply.
-depth
True when the level below the start of the file satisfies the given value (number).
A leading plus sign means greater than and a minus sign means less than for depth.
Combine -depth with the operators -and, -or and -not to build larger expressions.
Tests are evaluated from left to right and stop at the first one that fails.
Use -depth early in the expression when it rules out many files cheaply.
-flags
True when the file flags of the file satisfies the given value (flag list).
A leading plus sign means greater than and a minus sign means less than for flags.
Combine -flags with the operators -and, -or and -not to build larger expressions.
Tests are evaluated from left to right and stop at the first one that fails.
Use -flags early in the expression when it rules out many files cheaply.
-exec command {} ;
Run the command once per match, with the braces replaced by the path; a trailing plus runs it once for many matches, which is much faster on large trees.
-print0
Print each path followed by a zero byte so that names with spaces survive a pipe.
-delete
Remove each matching file or empty folder; test the expression with print first.

sections.body: zip [-r] archive file ...

sections.heading: DESCRIPTION
sections.body: Adds files to a zip archive; the recursive switch walks into folders.
